title: JPMorgan says Bitcoin could get more support than gold as ETF hedges unwind
body: JPMorgan says Bitcoin's hedging overhang could work in its favour against gold What happened JPMorgan analysts said in a note dated September 17 that Bitcoin could gain more support than gold if investors start unwinding the short positions and options currently used to hedge Bitcoin ETF holdings. The bank pointed to a gap in how the two ETF markets have recovered since inflows returned after the Federal Reserve's late-July meeting: gold ETFs have clawed back all of their earlier 2026 outflows, while Bitcoin ETFs have only recovered about half of theirs. The evidence behind the call is positioning data, not price action. Short interest in BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) remains close to its highest level this year, while short interest in the SPDR Gold Shares ETF (GLD) sits below its historical average. IBIT's put-to-call open interest ratio is also higher than GLD's, which JPMorgan reads as a sign that Bitcoin ETF investors are paying up for downside protection at a rate gold investors simply are not. Why it matters This is a mechanical argument about market positioning, not a fundamental case for Bitcoin over gold. JPMorgan's own framing is that Bitcoin still faces a more sceptical positioning backdrop than gold, likely due to more elevated hedging demand. The logic runs like this: a large pool of shorts and protective puts represents pressure that has to go somewhere.

title: Fed's unanimous hike stirs debate over how long high inflation persists
body: UBS's view that further hikes remain likely this year points to continued support for the US dollar and real yields, a combination that raises the opportunity cost of holding gold and could see some of August's ETF inflows unwind in the near term. Longer term, the bank argues gold's investment case remains intact, underpinned by rising global debt, an expected weaker dollar and the prospect of rate cuts next year. Other analysts framed the unanimous vote as evidence the Fed is taking a firmer stance against persistent inflation, much of it tied to elevated energy prices flowing from the conflict in the Middle East, with a further hike by year end widely seen as close to settled. Beyond that, views diverge sharply on how long above-target inflation could persist, with one long-term assessment suggesting price stability might not return for years given structural pressures from energy security, fiscal spending and the capital intensity of the AI investment cycle. -- The Fed hiked unanimously, but analysts can't agree on how long this inflation fight will last.

title: ICYMI: Trump tells Axios he's nearing a big decision on resuming Iran war
body: Trump's comments to Axios add a fresh layer of uncertainty to an oil market already struggling to price the war's trajectory, echoing JP Morgan's own admission this week that it has no clear baseline view for crude. A resumption of major US combat operations against Iran would raise the risk of further attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping, the scenario Saudi Arabia and Qatar are understood to have flagged when they helped persuade Trump to hold off in August. Conversely, any sign that Tuesday's meeting with Gulf leaders tilts toward renewed diplomacy could ease some of the risk premium currently built into oil prices, though traders are likely to treat that as a low probability outcome given Trump's repeated threats over recent months. With tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz still below pre-war levels despite the increased US naval presence, any escalation risk keeps a floor under prices even as the broader market leans on demand destruction rather than supply fears alone. --- Adam had the news on this earlier: Trump says he faces a "big decision" on whether to launch new attacks on Iran I'm doing a ICYMI here... title: Oil Slides for Third Session
body: Crude oil slipped toward $101 per barrel on Friday, extending losses for a third straight session as fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East eased and optimism grew over renewed diplomatic efforts to end the conflict and restore energy flows. Saudi Arabia aims to restore roughly half of the capacity on its East–West pipeline within days, with a full return to normal operations expected within six weeks. In the interim, the kingdom is diverting some crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz. To reduce exposure to potential Iranian attacks, shuttle vessels now move crude through the strait and transfer it to tankers waiting outside the area. Separate reports indicated that China has pressed Iran to help rein in Houthi militants after a request from Riyadh, following a surge in rebel attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to resume strikes on Iran ahead of a meeting with Gulf leaders in New York next week. title: Costa Rica Unemployment Rate Falls to 7.0% in Q2
body: Costa Rica's unemployment rate declined to 7.0% in the second quarter of 2026, down from 7.4% in the same period a year earlier, and slightly lower than 7.1% in the previous quarter. Nationwide, the number of unemployed was estimated at 164,000 people, of whom 98,000 were men and 66,000 were women. The unemployment rate stood at 6.8% for men and 7.2% for women. The labor force totaled 2.35 million people, comprising 1.43 million men and 921,000 women. The net labor force participation rate was 54.6% overall, broken down as 66.3% for men and 42.9% for women. Total employment rose to 2.18 million people, with an overall employment rate of 50.8%, including 61.7% for men and 39.8% for women. Informal employment reached 785,000 people, consisting of 438,000 self-employed workers and 348,000 wage earners or unpaid family helpers. title: New Zealand Equities Head for Weekly Gain
body: The NZX 50 rose 29 points, or 0.2%, to 13,785 in Friday morning trading, extending its advance to a third consecutive session. The move followed gains on Wall Street, as easing oil prices helped pull down US Treasury yields, even as the Federal Reserve's latest rate hike underscored its determination to rein in inflation. Sentiment remained supported by Thursday's data showing New Zealand's Q2 GDP grew faster than expected. Still, investors were cautious ahead of China's upcoming interest rate decision and next week's US PMI releases, which are expected to provide further guidance on the economic outlook in both economies. On the domestic data front, New Zealand's trade deficit narrowed in August compared with July, with exports rising more than imports, while food inflation held at a 19‑month low. Sector-wise, real estate, consumer discretionary, and financials were the main drivers of the benchmark index. Notable gainers included Port of Tauranga (up 1.0%), Chorus (up 0.8%), Hallenstein Glasson (up 0.8%), and Auckland International Airport (up 0.5%). title: New Zealand Food Inflation Stays at 19-Month Low
body: New Zealand's annual food inflation held at 1.9% in August 2026, unchanged from July and remaining at its lowest level since December 2024. Prices for meat, poultry, and fish rose 3.4% (up from 3.2% in July), rebounding from July's slowest growth rate since at least June 2025 and continuing to be the largest driver of the overall increase in food prices. Grocery food prices also picked up, rising 1.7% year-on-year (compared with 1.6% in July). In contrast, fruit and vegetable prices fell more sharply, dropping 1.6% after a 1.0% decline in July. On a monthly basis, food prices increased 0.3% in August, following a 0.1% rise in July, marking the fourth consecutive month of gains.
